TH.tipNote: With a 10% service charge on the bill, nothing more is needed; otherwise leave small change, around 20 baht.
TH.note: At '++' places the final bill is about 17% above the menu price; street food and local restaurants usually charge the menu price.
TH.serviceNote: Hotel restaurants and many upmarket venues add 10% service charge (and VAT on top); the consumer board says it is optional but must be displayed.

AE.name: United Arab Emirates
AE.tipNote: If a 10% service charge is on the bill, no tip is needed; otherwise 10% to 15% of the total is appreciated (Lonely Planet's Dubai guide says 5-10% is enough).
AE.note: The 5% VAT is inside the menu price; extra lines on a bill are the service charge and any municipality or tourism fee. Dubai's 7% municipality fee is suspended for now.
AE.serviceNote: Hotel restaurants usually add 10% and some standalone places do too (most do not). Visit Dubai says it often goes to the business, not the waiter. The menu or bill says.

IN.name: India
IN.tipNote: Tipping is customary but modest: 5% to 10% in cash, or round up, even if a service charge was on the bill.
IN.note: Many mid-range and upmarket menus list prices before tax ('plus taxes'), so the bill is at least 5% higher; street food and small places often quote final prices.
IN.serviceNote: Some restaurants still add 5% to 10% service charge, but it must be voluntary; you can ask for it to be removed.

AT.name: Austria
AT.tipNote: Round up or add 5-10% for good service, and tell the server the total you want to pay.
AT.serviceNote: Check the bill: if a tip is already included, don't pay it twice.

BE.name: Belgium
BE.tipNote: Service is already in the price; rounding up or leaving 5-10% is a nice touch but not required.
BE.serviceNote: Service is already included in the price.

BG.name: Bulgaria
BG.tipNote: Leave about 10% in cash for good service, more if you loved it.
BG.note: Bulgaria switched from the lev to the euro on 1 January 2026, so older guides may quote levs.

HR.name: Croatia
HR.tipNote: Round up in cafes and leave about 10% for a good restaurant meal.
HR.note: Sources differ: Lonely Planet's Croatia heading says at least 10%, its Europe guide says 5-10%.

CY.name: Cyprus
CY.tipNote: Tipping is up to you; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is a kind thank-you.

EE.name: Estonia
EE.tipNote: Round up, or leave about 10% when the food or service was exceptional.

FI.name: Finland
FI.tipNote: Service is always included, so don't add a tip; rounding up is welcome but never expected.
FI.note: VAT is already in the price.
FI.serviceNote: Service is always included in the bill.

FR.name: France
FR.tipNote: Service is already included, so a tip is optional: a few euros, up to about 10% for great service.
FR.note: The menu price is what you pay: taxes and service are included.
FR.serviceNote: Service is included by law in menu prices ('service compris').

DE.name: Germany
DE.tipNote: Round up to about 5-10% and tell the server the total you want to pay, instead of leaving cash on the table.
DE.note: Sources differ on the amount: visitBerlin says 10-15%, Lonely Planet says 5-10%.

GR.name: Greece
GR.tipNote: No tip is required; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated.
GR.note: Sources differ on service: Athens tourism says restaurants add none, Lonely Planet says it is normally included, so check the bill.

IE.name: Ireland
IE.tipNote: Not expected, but 10% for good service is customary; skip it if a service charge is already on the bill.
IE.serviceNote: Large parties (six or more) often get a service charge; the price list must say whether one applies.

IT.name: Italy
IT.tipNote: Tipping isn't expected here, so round up or leave a few euros only for great service.
IT.note: A regional law bans the coperto in Lazio (including Rome).
IT.serviceNote: Coperto (a flat table charge, around EUR 2 per person) is common and legal if shown on the menu; it is not a tip.

LV.name: Latvia
LV.tipNote: Round up the bill, or leave about 10% if you liked the service.

LT.name: Lithuania
LT.tipNote: Leave 5-15% depending on service, unless the bill already shows a service fee.

LU.name: Luxembourg
LU.tipNote: Service is already in the price; round up or leave 5-10% if you want to say thanks.
LU.note: Menu prices must include VAT and all other taxes by law.
LU.serviceNote: Restaurants must show prices with service included.

MT.name: Malta
MT.tipNote: Check the bill for a service charge first; if there is none, 5-10% for good service is reasonable, and rounding up is fine at a cafe.
MT.note: Malta's tourism authority calls a 5-10% tip customary for good service but not needed when a service charge is on the bill.
MT.serviceNote: Some restaurants add a service charge; if one is on the bill, no tip is needed.

NL.name: Netherlands
NL.tipNote: Locals often just round up; about 10% is plenty for a great meal.
NL.note: Holland.com calls about 10% quite acceptable but not fixed.

PT.name: Portugal
PT.tipNote: There's no big tipping culture: leave small change or round up, and about 10% only at fine dining.
PT.note: Starters brought unasked (couvert) are charged if you eat them; you can send them back.

SK.name: Slovakia
SK.tipNote: Round up the bill, usually by about 5-10%; it isn't mandatory.

SI.name: Slovenia
SI.tipNote: Tipping is not obligatory; rounding up is polite and 5-10% is a warm thank-you for good service.
SI.note: Guides disagree on size: Rough Guides says round up, Ljubljana.info says 10% or even 20% is a nice gesture.

ES.name: Spain
ES.tipNote: Tipping isn't customary; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is welcome.
ES.note: A sign saying 'IVA NO INCLUIDO' means 10% will be added to the bill.

GB.name: United Kingdom
GB.tipNote: If a 12.5% service charge is on the bill, don't add more; otherwise leave 10-15%.
GB.note: Pubs: tipping the bar staff isn't done.
GB.serviceNote: Usually 12.5%, shown on the bill; it is optional and you can ask to remove it.

CH.name: Switzerland
CH.tipNote: Service is included; rounding up or leaving about 10% is customary but you're not obliged.
CH.note: Menu prices are final prices in francs including VAT.
CH.serviceNote: Service is included in the price.

NO.name: Norway
NO.tipNote: Not expected; locals round up or leave 5-10% when they're happy.
NO.note: Visit Norway says tips tend to stay within 5-15%, Lonely Planet says restaurant tipping isn't expected at all.

SE.name: Sweden
SE.tipNote: Round up the bill (for example 280 to 300 SEK); about 10% is a nice tip on a larger meal.
SE.serviceNote: A service charge is sometimes included but is clearly stated on the bill.

DK.name: Denmark
DK.tipNote: Service is included in the bill; tip only if the service was great, there's no set amount.
DK.serviceNote: Service is included in restaurant bills.

IS.name: Iceland
IS.tipNote: Service is included, so tipping isn't expected; a small cash tip for great service is welcome.
IS.note: The stated price must include VAT by law.
IS.serviceNote: Service is already included in the bill at most restaurants and cafes.

PL.name: Poland
PL.tipNote: Leave about 10% for good service in a restaurant; for a coffee, a coin in the jar is plenty.

HU.name: Hungary
HU.tipNote: If 'szerviz' is on the bill, don't add more; otherwise tip about 10%, and say the total you want to pay.
HU.note: The 12.5% figure comes from a 2015 article, so check the bill.
HU.serviceNote: Many restaurants add a service charge of about 12.5%, shown as 'szerviz'; if it's there, add no tip.

TR.name: Turkey
TR.tipNote: Leave about 10% (15% for very good service), ideally in cash: since the ban some venues offer 8, 10 or 15% on the card machine, but many cannot take card tips.
TR.note: Menus must now show the full price: no service, table or cover charge may be added, and tips are voluntary.
TR.serviceNote: Since 30 January 2026 restaurants may not add service, table or cover charges under any name (Official Gazette 33153).

MX.name: Mexico
MX.tipNote: Tip about 10%, up to 15% for very good service; it's voluntary, so nobody can demand it.
MX.note: The usual tip is 10% (15% for very good service). Lonely Planet's Americas guide says 15-20% and that a service charge is common, but Profeco, Mexico City tourism and Lonely Planet's 2026 Mexico article point to 10%.
MX.serviceNote: By law no provider may demand a tip or set its amount.

BR.name: Brazil
BR.tipNote: If the 10% service fee is on the bill, pay it as your tip and don't add another.
BR.note: Tax inclusion in menu prices was not separately sourced.
BR.serviceNote: A 10% 'taxa de servico' is often printed on the bill; by law it is optional and must say so.

AR.name: Argentina
AR.tipNote: Leave about 10% in cash; it isn't a legal duty but it's a firm custom.
AR.note: Tax inclusion in menu prices could not be sourced (the national price-display PDF was unreadable); Lonely Planet says a service charge is more commonly added.
AR.serviceNote: Some restaurants charge a 'cubierto' per person; it can't be charged for children under 12.

CL.name: Chile
CL.tipNote: The bill suggests 10%; say 'con propina' to include it, or decline, it's voluntary.
CL.note: Menu prices must include IVA by law.
CL.serviceNote: The bill suggests a tip of at least 10%, but it is voluntary.

PE.name: Peru
PE.tipNote: Tipping isn't standard and many locals don't. If no 'servicio' or 'recargo' line is on the bill, about 10% is a kind gesture; if there is one, you've already tipped.
PE.note: The tax and price-display rules are official; the tipping size is a judgement because Lonely Planet's two Peru articles disagree and no tourism-board figure was found.
PE.serviceNote: Many mid-range and upscale restaurants add a 'servicio' or 'recargo al consumo' of up to 13% (Decreto Ley 25988); Indecopi says listed prices must include it. Check the menu and bill.

CO.name: Colombia
CO.tipNote: The bill may suggest 10%; it's voluntary, so you can accept, change it or decline.

CR.name: Costa Rica
CR.tipNote: The 10% service is already in the price, so an extra tip is optional; about 5% is appreciated for good service.
CR.note: By law the menu price must be the final price including 13% IVA and 10% service. If a menu says '+ impuestos' or '10% servicio no incluido' it breaks the rule and the bill would be about 23% higher.
CR.serviceNote: 10% table service, worked out before tax, must also be in the final menu price; not charged on takeaway.

DO.name: Dominican Republic
DO.tipNote: The 10% legal tip is already on the bill; the tourism board says a further 10% is customary.
DO.note: Whether menus show prices before tax and service was not verified.
DO.serviceNote: A legal 10% tip is added to dine-in bills (not takeout or delivery).

CU.name: Cuba
CU.tipNote: Check for a 10-12% service charge on the bill; if there's none, tip the waiter a little (a tour operator suggests about 10% or small change).
CU.note: Low confidence: no official source on taxes, menu pricing or service charges could be read. Private restaurants price in pesos at informal rates and many accept euros; ask which currency the menu uses.
CU.serviceNote: Service charges of 10-12% are fairly common in state restaurants and smarter paladares; some add a flat 10%.

JM.name: Jamaica
JM.tipNote: Check the bill for a gratuity first; if there is none, tip 15-20% in a restaurant. Card machines may offer tips up to 25%.
JM.note: GCT and a service charge are often added to the bill rather than the menu price, at least in hotels. The only tipping sources are a newspaper and Lonely Planet's Caribbean advice; no Jamaica Tourist Board page could be read.
JM.serviceNote: Some restaurants add a compulsory 10-20% service charge or gratuity; check the bill before tipping.

JP.name: Japan
JP.tipNote: Tipping isn't the custom and can confuse staff.
JP.note: Menus must show tax-inclusive prices since April 2021.
JP.serviceNote: A service charge is generally added to the final bill in restaurants.

KR.name: South Korea
KR.tipNote: Tipping isn't the custom and some staff will refuse it.
KR.note: Sources differ on whether VAT is in menu prices: a 2012 rule says it must be, Visit Seoul says it is 'added on'.
KR.serviceNote: Many hotels and upscale restaurants add a 10% service charge on top of VAT.

CN.name: China
CN.tipNote: Tipping isn't expected; check the bill for a service charge first.
CN.note: Tax inclusion in menu prices was not separately sourced.
CN.serviceNote: Quality and high-end restaurants may add a 5-15% service charge.

HK.name: Hong Kong
HK.tipNote: Most restaurants add 10% service, so you needn't tip on top.
HK.note: Hong Kong has no sales tax or VAT.
HK.serviceNote: Most restaurants add a 10% service charge; some cafes and diners don't.

TW.name: Taiwan
TW.tipNote: Tipping isn't expected; a 10% service charge is often added to the bill.
TW.note: Tax inclusion in menu prices was not separately sourced.
TW.serviceNote: A 10% service charge is customary at hotels and restaurants.

VN.name: Vietnam
VN.tipNote: Tipping isn't expected in restaurants; rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is welcome, and nothing extra if a service charge is on the bill.
VN.note: The Law on Prices says listed prices include taxes and fees, but upmarket places may quote prices before VAT and service, so check the menu footnote. No official source on service charges was found.
VN.serviceNote: Check the bill for a service charge or VAT line.

PH.name: Philippines
PH.tipNote: If a service charge is on the bill, no tip is needed; otherwise rounding up or leaving 5-10% for good service is appreciated.
PH.note: VAT is 12%; some restaurants roll it into menu prices and others add it to the bill, and the menu says which. No Department of Tourism tipping page could be read.
PH.serviceNote: Many restaurants add a 5-10% service charge; the law sets no rate but all of it must go to non-managerial staff.

KH.name: Cambodia
KH.tipNote: Tipping isn't a custom; rounding up or leaving a dollar or two for good service is plenty, and nothing if a service charge is on the bill.
KH.note: Prices are often in US dollars. Whether menu prices include the 10% VAT could not be sourced, so check the menu footnote.
KH.serviceNote: Hotels and restaurants commonly add a 10% service charge (Ministry of Tourism FAQ); Rough Guides says 5-10% at higher-end places.

AU.name: Australia
AU.tipNote: Not expected; for table service in a city restaurant, 10% is appreciated, nothing at the counter.
AU.note: Tourism Australia says restaurants add no service charge; the holiday surcharge is separate.
AU.serviceNote: Some venues add a weekend or public-holiday surcharge of up to 15% (Lonely Planet); check the menu.

NZ.name: New Zealand
NZ.tipNote: Tipping isn't expected, though 10% for really good table service is welcome.
NZ.note: Lonely Planet says some venues add a holiday surcharge of up to 15%.

ZA.name: South Africa
ZA.tipNote: Tip 10-15% for good service; skip it if a group service charge is on the bill.
ZA.note: South African Tourism's page is from 2018, and VAT inclusion in menu prices could not be sourced.
ZA.serviceNote: A 10% service charge is added automatically for tables of more than six guests.

MA.name: Morocco
MA.tipNote: Check the bill for a service charge first; if there is none, leave 5-10%, or up to 15% at upscale places.
MA.note: Menu prices must include VAT (Law 31-08). The Moroccan tourist office has no tipping page; tipping sources are a publisher, a news site and a local guide, and the first sets 10-15% where the others say 5-10%.
MA.serviceNote: Popular tourist restaurants often add 10% (Lonely Planet, Le360); no legal rate found.

EG.name: Egypt
EG.tipNote: A service charge is usually added, so leave a little extra in cash for the waiter; about 10% if there is none.
EG.note: A 2020 chamber statement says tourist-establishment menus must show all-inclusive prices, but a 2023 report says diners pay 26% (12% service, 14% VAT) on top. Assume tax and service are added until the menu says otherwise.
EG.serviceNote: About 12% service is added in tourist establishments (Lonely Planet says 10%).

IL.name: Israel
IL.tipNote: Tip 10-12% for good service and 15% for excellent (15% is the norm in Tel Aviv), ideally in cash.
IL.note: No Ministry of Tourism tipping page could be read; the three tipping sources (a hotel-chain blog, a news magazine, a community travel wiki) agree on 10-15%.
IL.serviceNote: Restaurants almost never add a service charge, except for large groups.

JO.name: Jordan
JO.tipNote: Tip about 10% on top of the bill, unless a service charge is already on it.
JO.note: Menu prices usually exclude the 16% sales tax and any 10% service line, so a bill can run up to about a quarter above the menu total.
JO.serviceNote: Many restaurants add a 10% 'service' line; it is a custom, not set by law.

QA.name: Qatar
QA.tipNote: A service charge is usually in the bill; an extra 10-15% in cash is appreciated.
QA.note: Tax inclusion in menu prices was not sourced.
QA.serviceNote: Most hospitality outlets include a service charge in the bill.

SA.name: Saudi Arabia
SA.tipNote: Servers generally expect a 10-15% tip at the end of the meal.
SA.note: Tipping is not mandatory and no service charge is added, so a 10-15% tip is not doubled up.
SA.serviceNote: Restaurants may not add service charges (Ministry of Commerce decision, reconfirmed 2017).

KE.name: Kenya
KE.tipNote: Tipping isn't required, but about 10% of the bill for a good meal is appreciated.
KE.note: VAT is 16% and licensed tourism businesses also pay a 2% levy on food and drink sales. No law on menu pricing was found, so check the menu for 'inclusive of VAT'.

TZ.name: Tanzania
TZ.tipNote: About 10% is customary at restaurants, up to 15% for very good service; always in cash.
TZ.note: Prices advertised by VAT-registered businesses must include 18% VAT. No Tanzania Tourist Board tipping page could be read; the tipping sources are safari operators and Lonely Planet's Africa guide.
